articles.title: North Korea launches 'suspected ballistic missile' into East Sea
articles.body:
In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.
North Korea on Sunday carried out a launch of a "suspected ballistic missile," the Japanese Prime Minister's office said, while South Korea's military reported that Pyongyang had fired an "unidentified projectile" into the East Sea.
In an update later in the day, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said North Korea had launched "at least one ballistic missile from near its eastern coast towards the northeast" at around 3 pm local time.
"We estimate that the ballistic missile reached a maximum altitude of approximately 60 km, flew a distance of approximately 440 km, and fell outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ)," he said.
It comes after North Korea this week rejected a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against its nuclear programme.
A spokesperson for the country's Foreign Ministry said the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution had "no effect on the DPRK's position as a nuclear weapons state."
In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship.
"You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.
Trump announced at the time that he also intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan - which would be their first meeting since Trump's first term in the White House.
On Friday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said he was "urging" Trump to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang, adding that Seoul was working to facilitate talks between the North and the US.
"I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality," he said of the potential for a meeting between US and North Korean officials.
However, hopes for an imminent meeting may have been doused slightly after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, criticised recent military drills in the Western Pacific, which she labelled a "US-led war rehearsal."
The US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up Exercise Freedom Edge 26, which US Pacific Command said advanced "trilateral readiness across the Indo-Pacific," on 11 September.
"Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," Kim Yo Jong added in a statement shared by North Korea's KCNA state news agency on Friday.

articles.title: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato
articles.body:
European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.
The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia.
The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war.
In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”.
Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands.
“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
“It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.
Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies.
On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X.
Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said.
Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato.
After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said.
However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it.
As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months.
Moscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago.
Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said.
In recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations.
“I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added.
All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence.
“To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said.
Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added.
Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said.
Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

articles.title: Hundreds of drones target Moscow on last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary election
articles.body:
Ukraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack that involved hundreds of drones.
The attack killed at least three people and damaged what Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said was one of Russia’s “key oil industry facilities” on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.
Zelenskyy said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, initially thought to be a short-range ballistic missile, but which sources said later was a winged drone.
The president did not offer any further details, prompting media reports in Ukraine that it was a ballistic missile, only for doubt to be cast on the weapon identification later in the day.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep inside Russia and has the range to reach the country’s capital.
Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels posted images of what they said was debris from a Flamingo missile found in the Moscow region, though the claims could not be independently verified. Ruslan Leviev, the head of the open-source investigation group Conflict Intelligence Team, said the debris probably came from a Flamingo missile.
Moscow’s mayor, Sergey Sobyanin, said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, though these figures are often exaggerated, and Ukraine’s daily drone fire rate estimated a number in the low hundreds.
Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election in Russia that is expected to tighten Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
At least three people were killed, including a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man, in separate incidents.
A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drone’s origin.
Kyiv has stepped up its campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil-refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.
A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties were reported and emergency services were on the scene. The refinery had already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.
The Pelican missile was initially thought to be the FP-7 made by Fire Point, Ukraine’s most successful long-range drone and missile maker. But several hours later, as the speculation persisted, other military sources said it was a long-range drone.
The company is also developing the longer-range FP-9, which has a range of more than 500 miles, meaning it could be used to target Moscow in the future. A test flight is expected later this autumn.
The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: MP: US criminal act in Lamerd and Minab is a modern example of crimes in Hiroshima and Nagasa
articles.body:
MP: US criminal act in Lamerd and Minab is a modern example of crimes in Hiroshima and Nagasa
TEHRAN — Iran’s Deputy Parliament Speaker Hamid Reza Haji Babaei has lashed out at the United States over its deadly strikes against civilian targets in southern Iran, declaring Washington’s strikes on the city of Lamerd and the Shajareh Tayyebah school in Minab as direct modern manifestations of the atomic atrocities perpetrated against Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Speaking during an open parliamentary session on Sunday, Haji Babaei reiterated Tehran’s resolve to hold the United States legally and politically accountable for blatant violations of international law and international humanitarian statutes.
“The criminal action of the United States in Lamerd and the Shajareh Tayyebah school in Minab is a textbook example of modern-day crimes akin to what transpired in Hiroshima and Nagasaki,” Haji Babaei said in response to a parliamentary notice raised by Musa Mousavi, the lawmaker representing Lamerd and Mohr.
“This is the exact same course of savagery, merely updated with modern technology and weapon systems. It demonstrates that the US continues to expand its repertoire of war crimes and brutality against sovereign nations while brazenly trampling basic human values,” the deputy speaker emphasized.
During his address on the Majlis floor, Musa Mousavi detailed the horrific dimensions of the strike on Lamerd, characterizing it as an indisputable war crime aimed deliberately at maximizing human suffering.
According to Mousavi, four precision-guided ballistic missiles—identified as Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM)—were fired into Lamerd, tearing through two residential neighborhoods and a public indoor sports arena.
Mousavi explained that the munitions deployed in Lamerd were designed specifically for wide-area lethality rather than standard structural demolition. Instead of detonating upon ground impact, the warheads exploded roughly 40 meters in the air, releasing an indiscriminate hail of 180,000 tungsten fragments per missile over a 360-degree radius.
“In total, 720,000 tungsten pellets were rained down on Lamerd. In a city of 30,000 people, this amounts to an average of 24 lethal projectiles for every single resident,” Mousavi noted, presenting photographs of perforated walls, doors, and residential infrastructure pockmarked with hundreds of shrapnel holes.
The lawmaker underscored that several factors prevented a significantly larger catastrophe beyond the recorded toll of 21 martyrs and 60 injured: the attack struck near the evening Iftar when families were indoors, the residential zones were less congested, and a neighboring school complex was empty at that hour.
Mousavi slammed the provocative rhetoric from US military commanders who praised the deployment of these weapons to “put pressure on the Iranian populace,” while highlighting how arms contractors such as Lockheed Martin subsequently saw inflated multibillion-dollar procurement contracts.
Echoing the directives of the Leader—who instructed the Iranian Judiciary to vigorously pursue legal cases against the United States over the carnage in Lamerd and Minab—Mousavi called on Iranian diplomats to turn these strikes into an international indictment against Washington across multilateral bodies.
The attacks on Lamerd and Minab represent some of the most devastating strikes on civilian infrastructure in southern Iran, sparking worldwide outrage and international scrutiny over Washington’s unlawful targeting methodologies.
The Tragedy of Shajareh Tayyebah
 
 Located in the eastern coastal plain of Hormozgan Province near the Strait of Hormuz, Minab is an ancient agricultural and trade hub, home to roughly 75,000 residents.
On February 28, the civilian population of Minab suffered one of the deadliest single mass-casualty attacks when a US cruise missile pulverized the Shajareh Tayyebah Elementary School during morning classes. The strike brought down the multi-story educational facility, martyring nearly 170 civilians—the vast majority of them young schoolchildren.
Independent investigations and a formal report by the United Nations Fact-Finding Mission concluded that the strike constituted an indiscriminate attack and a potential war crime. Inquiries revealed that US forces had relied on decades-old, obsolete intelligence regarding a nearby historical installation, failing to take basic precautions to verify the presence of active educational institutions.
Lamerd, situated in the southernmost tip of Fars Province near the Persian Gulf energy corridor, is a strategic hub of energy, aluminum manufacturing, and commerce. Bordering Bushehr and Hormozgan, the county sits atop major natural gas fields, including the Tabnak and Eram reservoirs, and hosts the sprawling Lamerd Special Economic Zone (housing the South Aluminum Corporation, SALCO).
Despite its purely civilian and economic profile, residential districts and civic sports infrastructure inside Lamerd were subjected to air-burst tungsten fragmentation strikes. Rather than striking isolated strategic installations, the deployment of anti-personnel fragmentation warheads over residential quarters underscored a calculated attempt to inflict maximum civilian terror.

articles.title: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles in three hours: South Korean military
articles.body:
North Korea yesterday launched two missiles off its eastern coast, its second set of tests in about a week and days after Pyongyang accused the US of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills.
Just three hours after launching a short-range ballistic missile toward the Sea of Japan (known as the “East Sea” in South Korea and the “East Sea of Korea” in North Korea) yesterday afternoon, North Korea fired another short-range ballistic missile, the South Korean Ministry of National Defense said.
If the subsequent launch is confirmed to be a ballistic missile, it would mark two consecutive ballistic missile tests by North Korea within a three-hour window.
Photo: AFP
The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the first test firing from the Wonsan area at about 3pm, identifying the weapon as a ballistic missile.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense also said it appeared to be a ballistic missile.
Japanese public broadcaster NHK said the projectile had come down outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.
The first projectile flew approximately 450km and is presumed to belong to the Hwasong-11 series, the South Korean military said.
The second short-range missile, which was also fired from Wonsan at about 5:50pm, flew more than 600km, it said.
“South Korean and US intelligence authorities have been tracking and sharing related developments from the initial stage of the launch, and have also shared information regarding the ‘North Korean ballistic missile’ with Japan,” the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said.
The South Korean National Security Council condemned the short-range missile launch, which follows a test on Sept. 12. The council urged Pyongyang to immediately cease missile activity, warning the test directly contravened UN Security Council resolutions.
Japan also lodged a protest through embassy channels in Beijing, a Nikkei report said.
“This series of North Korean actions threatens the peace and security of Japan, the region, and the international community,” Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi was quoted as saying by Nikkei.
On Saturday, North Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang’s nuclear program.
Pyongyang last week also condemned a US-led naval drill which included South Korea and Japan and which ran from Aug. 29 to Sept. 10 near Guam.
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s sister, Kim Yo-jong, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for “ever-worsening” tensions on the Korean Peninsula and vowed no change in the country’s course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

articles.title: US envoy highlights AI rivalry with China, warns against domestic innovation caps
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
20 September 2026•Update: 20 September 2026
The US faces a more complex challenge from China in competing for artificial intelligence (AI) than it did during the Cold War, when the two countries had fewer economic ties, US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Sunday.
"Unlike in the Cold War or any other adversary we've had in the past—Germany, Japan, etc.—we've never been so intertwined economically with a competitor or potential adversary like we are with the People's Republic of China, so it is a much more complex situation," Waltz told US television network CNN.
Waltz indicated that Washington sees space for narrow bilateral guardrails during an upcoming summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, pointing to rules regarding algorithmic diffusion, nuclear weapons systems, and keeping humans in command loops.
However, he drew a firm line against domestic regulatory limits. "What we cannot do is put a throttle on our innovators, on our entrepreneurs, on so many great Americans in our system that's so unique that are creating the solutions of the future," Waltz said.
Arctic security and polar trade corridors
Addressing northern defense, Waltz framed a new security agreement between the US and Denmark over Greenland as an urgent requirement for strategic early warning.
"If we're ever attacked by any type of intercontinental missiles, they'll come over the Arctic," Waltz explained, stressing that radar and sensor installations in the region require robust protection and unrestricted access.
The envoy connected northern access to continental missile defense systems, an icebreaker pact reached with Finland, expanded military spending within NATO, and resource extraction across polar energy and critical mineral reserves.
He noted that retreating ice leads shipping to bypass southern chokepoints and traverse Arctic routes, making diplomatic pacts with Denmark and Greenland essential to safeguarding the High North.
Maritime defense and Iran war pressure
Turning to Middle Eastern waterways, Waltz said the US and its allies will take "decisive action" against any actors disrupting civilian maritime traffic across the Bab al-Mandeb, Strait of Hormuz, and Suez Canal.
Responding to reports that military confrontations could stretch toward 2029, Waltz said time favors Washington.
He explained that sanctions will remain indefinite until verified nuclear and behavioral concessions take place, claiming that the pressure directly targets Tehran's power structure because the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) controls 40% to 50% of the Iranian economy.
Meanwhile, CNN reported that the Trump administration prefers that Saudi Arabia counter the push rather than using American force directly.
A US official told the network that Washington is expanding targeting data and intelligence sharing with Riyadh, while sources noted Saudi officials expressed confidence in their forces following a decade of training.

articles.title: CIA chief meets Egypt's Sisi in Cairo amid ongoing regional wars
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
CIA chief meets Egypt's Sisi in Cairo amid ongoing regional wars
US Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi Sunday in a rare visit to Cairo, as the United States warned of rapid escalation in the Middle East war.
Sisi's office said the meeting, attended by Egypt's intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, discussed the wars in Iran, the Gaza Strip and Sudan, as well as attacks on Gulf countries and threats to maritime security.
Sisi stressed "the paramount importance of settling regional crises through political and diplomatic tracks," according to a presidency statement.
It comes after the US State Department warned Americans against travel to the region, as hostilities rage between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis.
"This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," it warned.
The violence has already disrupted air and marine traffic, as well as energy exports, pushing global oil prices past $100 a barrel.
Ratcliffe's visit comes days after de facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met Sisi in Cairo.
The pair urged safe and secure maritime navigation through Bab al-Mandab, after the Houthis seized the Yemeni coast in a lightning offensive.
US media last week reported Washington refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.
Washington then approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats", the US State Department said.
Cairo is a key US ally in the region and one of the top recipients of US military aid.
It has repeatedly positioned itself as a stabilising force in a turbulent region, keeping open lines of communication with rival sides, including Israel, Hamas and Iran.
Sisi's office said Ratcliffe on Sunday "lauded Egypt's pivotal role in supporting efforts aimed at reaching peaceful, comprehensive settlements to regional crises".

Ukraine Launches Retaliatory Strikes on Moscow Refinery Supplying 40% of Region’s Petroleum Product Demand
In response to the Russian military aggression, Ukrainian strike drones and cruise missiles hit the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya overnight on September 20, sparking a large-scale fire at the plant.
Footage of the strike was published by the monitoring channel Exilenova+, which Militarnyi cited on September 20. The attack ignited a blaze on the refinery grounds, with further consequences still being assessed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Monitoring resources logged a drone-danger alert at 3:19 a.m. By 3:51, Russian channels reported air defenses engaging over the capital region, and interceptor activity continued past 5:27 a.m., according to Militarnyi.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on social media that Russian air defenses had destroyed 151 drones overnight, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Emergency crews were working at sites where debris had fallen, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the operation in a post on X. He wrote: "Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. One of Russia's key oil industry facilities and the aggressor's logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine."
Zelenskyy added that "the systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen, and Pelican." He did not tie individual systems to specific targets. The president also noted the strike affected a facility in the Voronezh region.
Geolocation of the footage indicated the strike damaged installations at the refinery:
- a combined crude-oil processing unit, known as the KUPN;
- the ELOU AVT-6 primary distillation installation.
A separate fire broke out at the "Sofyino" logistics technopark, matching the logistics facility Zelenskyy referenced.
Among the systems Zelenskyy listed was the FP-5 Flamingo, a Ukrainian long-range missile. Near the refinery, local residents recovered debris from an unidentified missile visually resembling the FP-5, and one video captured the sound of a jet engine, Militarnyi reported. Its use at the site remained unconfirmed.
The Kapotnya plant ranks among Russia's ten largest refineries and supplies roughly 40% of the Moscow region's petroleum products, per Militarnyi. It processes up to 11 million tons of crude annually across more than 30 technological units, including catalytic and thermal cracking and reforming lines.
The facility produces AI-80EK, AI-92EK, and AI-95EK gasolines, diesel, aviation kerosene, bitumen, sulfur, and polymers, the outlet noted.
The strike extends a sustained Ukrainian campaign against Russia's military aggression. On August 28, FP-1 drones set fires at the Slavneft-YANOS refinery in Yaroslavl, the largest oil-processing site in Russia's Central Federal District, in an attack that killed one person and injured 27. Weeks earlier, on August 5, a drone raid ignited a blaze at Rosneft's Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa, more than 1,400 kilometers from Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine launches 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds fired at Moscow
articles.body:
Ukraine launches 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds fired at Moscow in what mayor describes as "largest ever" attack
Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds that were launched toward Moscow, officials said Sunday as the Kremlin was wrapping up the third and last day of its parliamentary elections.
Moscow's mayor described the wave of drones as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital and said there had been damage to a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.
Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv had used a range of missiles and drones in the attack — including Ukraine's domestically made Flamingo and Pelican missiles — to hit oil and logistics facilities.
"These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine," Zelenskyy said, referring to the financial pressure that Kyiv hopes to put on Russia's economy.
Ukraine also continued to fend off Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said. A Russian drone strike hit a monastery in Ukraine's Kherson region Saturday, killing a member of the clergy and wounding four people, he said.
A Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital also killed two children and their mother on Saturday evening, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional state administration. He later said that another child wounded in the same attack had died in hospital on Sunday.
The U.S. State Department on Friday said it had approved a potential $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine. The news came as President Trump signed a bill introducing new sanctions designed to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, after Congress gave its approval following months of delay.
Mr. Trump and Zelenskyy spoke on Sunday and have agreed to meet in New York, the Ukrainian president said on social media.
"This meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," he said. "There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life. We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps."
Russia votes in an election devoid of opposition
The attack took place on the final day of Russia's first wartime parliamentary election — balloting that has been virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and is all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.
Russia was also holding the vote in the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still doesn't fully control, and in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv has denounced the action as illegal.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down a total of 1,110 Ukrainian drones across the country, as well as over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 450 drones had been destroyed en route to the Russian capital, and that the attack had damaged the Moscow Oil Refinery and a residential building.
He said the "unprecedented attack" on Moscow was an attempt to disrupt the elections. "The enemy failed in this regard," he said.
Since Russia's invasion more than four years ago, Ukraine has become a global leader in military drone technology, deploying domestically produced long-range drones alongside missiles for strikes deep inside Russia. Its drone technology has impressed governments and defense manufacturers around the world.
Kyiv is aiming to make the Russian public feel the war's consequences and pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiating a peace settlement. Putin has so far shown no signs he intends to stop the invasion.
Instead, Moscow and Kyiv have been drawn into an escalating duel of long-range aerial strikes as fighting along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line in eastern and southern Ukraine has slowed, restricted by large numbers of drones and ground robots threatening troop movements.

articles.title: Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production
articles.body:
Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production
Documents obtained by POLITICO show a Russian state company blueprint for increasing drone carbon fiber production as the Kremlin escalates air war over Europe.
Satellite images captured in May (L) and July (R) show land adjacent to Rosatom's Alabuga-Volokno carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan's Alabuga Special Economic Zone being cleared for the expansion project. | Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre
Moscow is moving to expand its capacity to make tens of thousands of the killer drones it deploys in attacks on Ukrainian cities, according to plans from a Russian state company obtained by POLITICO.
The expansion of state firm Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno factory in Russia’s Tatarstan region would allow Moscow to make an additional 500 tons of military-grade aerospace carbon fiber each year by 2029. The strong lightweight material is key to building the drone’s airframe.
The production increase would translate to an additional 28,000 weaponized drones every year, according to one expert estimate — a 78% increase in production of weapons like the one that struck a passenger train on the Polish border this month and others that have left scores of Ukrainian civilians dead. Ukraine estimates Russia can currently produce more than 36,000 kamikaze drones, known as “Gerans,” annually.
Advertisement
The plans underscore Russia's commitment to weaponized drone technology to power its war machine, which it is increasingly turning against the rest of Europe.
The Alabuga-Volokno factory and its parent company, Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX, are sanctioned by the U.K., U.S. and multiple other Western governments.
The factory is a key node in Moscow’s military-industrial supply chain and is the same one that received a disguised shipment of 46 tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from a Chinese-state corporation earlier this year, according to internal Rosatom shipping and customs documents reported earlier this month by POLITICO. Rosatom previously said the firm and its subsidiaries “operate in full compliance” with applicable laws and regulations.
Police experts examine fragments of a drone which targeted a commuter train, killing one and wounding eight people, in the Kharkiv region on September 18, 2026 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Sergey Bobok/ AFP via Getty Images
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that it was unaware of the Russian drone production expansion plans and “strictly controls exports of dual use items in accordance with law.”
Business, design and structural plans gathered from Russian sources by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre — a Kyiv-based think tank close to the Ukrainian government — detail the factory’s expansion and schematics for its equipment and construction.
Rosatom declined to comment on the documents.
Advertisement
The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are authentic, according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record.
Russia's drone war expands
In May, the Russian government approved Rosatom’s plans to build the new line at its Alabuga-Volokno factory “for the production of chemical fibers and threads” to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber per year, according to official approval for the construction project.
Satellite images between May and July show land earmarked for the expansion project adjacent to Alabuga-Volokno’s current carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan being cleared for construction, said the Ukrainian official. The images provided by the USCC show “proof that it is already growing,” this official said.
The foundation of the new factory “is being prepared,” said weapons expert David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank, who independently obtained satellite images of the site from August. The timeline for the factory’s completion in 2027, he said, “requires rapid construction.”
Drones allow Moscow to “launch these massive volleys and put pressure on deep targets within Ukraine at many different locations, and ensure that they can saturate the defenses,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a former adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense who researches drone warfare at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. “It's been a very good coercive tool and critical to Russia's deep strike campaign.”
Rosatom’s plans to grow its capacity to feed Russia’s demands to increase weaponized drone production isn’t just a concern for Ukraine as Moscow’s fifth year of all-out war drags into another winter.
Advertisement
“The expansion of Alabuga and its affiliated enterprises should be viewed not merely as a problem for the Ukrainian front, but as a long-term challenge to the security of the whole of Europe,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre.
Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno will aid this national effort. The three key reasons for expanding the factory include “import substitution of dual-use products” and “meeting the demand of Russian strategic sectors (aviation, defense industry) for carbon fiber,” according to the Rosatom documents.
The factory’s total capacity “could make 28,000 Shahed 136 drone airframes,” calculates weapons expert Albright, whose Institute for Science and International Security has conducted years of in-depth research on Russia’s drone production. Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones are based on the design of Iran’s Shahed.
“Without the carbon fiber, they can't make the drone,” Albright said. Russia “can't substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down,” he explained, noting the material is used to strengthen the wing and internal structures, such as those for the fuel tank and engine.
Moscow is not getting enough polyacrylonitrile tow — a so-called PAN-precursor — used to make high-spec carbon fiber “for all their defense needs,” Albright said. Through the factory, Moscow is attempting to reduce its reliance on imports of the fibrous chemical essential to reinforcing its drones’ airframe.
Advertisement
The internal Rosatom plans show the firm intends to build a new “a modern PAN plant” in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone factory complex. “The project's primary product will be UMT42S-3K grade carbon fiber,” the documents detail, to be “used in the aerospace industry.”
Metadata scraped from the document shows it was created by an employee of Russian state corporation Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX at the end of last year.
Drones produced in the Alabuga SEZ complex have become a key part of Moscow’s strategy of targeting both the Ukrainian military and civilians.
“Monitoring, restricting the supply of critical components, sanctions enforcement, disrupting logistics chains and reducing the production resilience of this complex must be among the priorities of the joint policy of Ukraine and its European partners,” said USCC’s Kuzan.
“At this stage, the Kremlin’s hybrid aggression is increasingly shifting towards direct escalation, particularly through the conduct of so-called sub-threshold actions, aimed at gauging the reaction of European countries,” he said, pointing to documented violations by Russian drones of Polish and Romanian airspace. Moscow has now also added jet engines to Russia’s design of its Geran drones — allowing it to strike further and faster.
Drones manufactured in the Russian Alabuga Special Economic Zone, Kuzan warned, “are likely to become the main instrument of the Russian Federation’s future campaigns in Europe.”
Advertisement
The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Europe at risk
With no end in sight for the Ukraine war and as Russia increases its attacks at NATO's eastern fringe, world leaders gather this week in New York City for the annual United Nations General Assembly.
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attends the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, 2026. | Alexander Kazavok/ AFP via Getty Images
Early this month, Russia’s permanent representative to the U.N., Vasily Nebenzya, reportedly led an unsuccessful effort to remove an item titled the “Situation in the Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine” from the upcoming UNGA agenda.
Revelations of the carbon fiber factory’s planned expansion mean Lavrov’s overtures should be approached with skepticism, said Nicholas Fenton, associate director for the Europe, Russia and Eurasia Program at CSIS.
The September drone attack on the passenger train close to the Polish border and a series of examples of hybrid warfare in Europe — like sabotage and other tactics that fall below the threshold of open warfare — show Moscow has “significant appetite” to escalate the conflict both in Ukraine and Europe, Fenton said.
Advertisement
“No matter the political outcome over some sort of diplomatic solution to Ukraine, we don't see Russia de-escalating when it comes to its military posture vis-à-vis NATO or vis-à-vis Europe,” Fenton said. “We believe that the current leadership of the regime in Russia is committed to confrontation with the West,” he said — even if a peace deal is struck.
At the start of September, President Donald Trump dispatched U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv to jumpstart a peace process. These visits reaped “substantive progress including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Witkoff wrote online afterward. Yet Russia killed five people in missile and drone attacks on Kyiv just a day after Trump's envoys left. Moscow has continued drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine since.
“The Russians are gaining momentum in the air war, continuing to iterate these systems, continuing to expand production,” Fenton said. “There's significant concern over what might be coming.”
Graham Lanktree reported from London. Phelim Kine reported from Washington.

articles.title: Zelensky Confirms Strikes on Moscow Refinery and Logistics Facilities
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces conducted major long-range strikes targeting key oil refining and logistics facilities in the Moscow region overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Sunday, Sept. 20.
“Our long-range responses worked very noticeably in the Moscow region tonight. Key oil industry and logistics facilities supporting the aggressor’s war machine were hit,” Zelensky wrote on social media.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky stated that Ukrainian forces deployed various long-range strike systems, including FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichnevyi, and Pelican. Ukrainian forces also hit an industrial facility in Russia’s Voronezh region.
He expressed gratitude to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS), the Special Operations Forces (SSO), the Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR), and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) for the joint operation.
“Moscow should stop building layered air defense rings at the expense of other regions and instead end its cruel war and choose peace,” Zelensky said, pointing to proposed de-escalation steps in energy and food security.
What facilities were damaged in the Moscow attack?
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed hitting the Gazprom Neft Moscow Oil Refinery in the Kapotnya district, roughly 15 kilometers from the Kremlin.
According to the General Staff, long-range strikes hit the AVT-6 primary crude processing unit, an integrated oil refining unit, and an isomerization unit, sparking a large fire across the plant. Long-range Alpha drones from the SBU flew over 500 kilometers to breach Russian air defenses and strike the facility.
NATO Ready for Any Russian Escalation, Military Chief Says
The Moscow Oil Refinery processes more than 11.6 million metric tons of crude oil annually, supplying roughly 35 to 40 percent of the fuel needs for Moscow and up to 70 percent of gasoline and aviation kerosene used across the wider Moscow region.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed Russian air defense units intercepted over 1,600 drones across all lines, including about 450 heading toward Moscow, calling the barrage the most massive Ukrainian drone assault on the capital to date.
Geolocated footage verified by independent media confirmed an extensive fire at the refining complex. Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported at least two deaths and six injuries in the surrounding province.
Additionally, Ukrainian defense technology firm Fire Point confirmed that FP-1 attack drones destroyed a commercial storage complex operated by Modern Warehouse Technologies in Sofyino, within the Ramensky district.

articles.title: Russia's ruling party on track to win election after Ukraine's drone attacks on Moscow
articles.body:
Russia's ruling party on track to win election after Ukraine's drone attacks on Moscow
Russia's ruling United Russia party on Sunday was projected to win the country's tightly controlled parliamentary elections, according to exit polls. Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on Moscow, killing three people, said city officials, on the third and final day of Russia's wartime vote.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Russia's ruling United Russia party was on track to easily win a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in Ukraine, partial official results showed on Sunday, after Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on the Russian capital.
In a tightly controlled political system which critics say does not tolerate genuine dissent, initial results showed United Russia comfortably ahead with 57.5% of the vote. Other parties like the Communists, the ultra-nationalist LDPR, the New People party and the Just Russia party – who all vote the same way as United Russia on major issues – trailed by a huge margin but were on course to win seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council and a former president, was quick to declare that United Russia had performed with dignity, a result he said showed that Russians had entrusted it to govern further.
Watch more'Election without meaningful competition': Russia’s results won't measure support for Putin or war
Russian government officials accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the State Duma vote - the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 – after Kyiv launched hundreds of drones at Moscow and other regions in what the TASS state news agency said was the biggest attack of its kind since the war began.
The drone strikes killed three people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine's Kherson region, including an election official, according to the region's governor and the election commission.
Read moreRussia vows to ‘intensify’ strikes on Kyiv after Ukraine’s election-day drone attacks
A facility at Moscow's oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged. As voting got underway in the capital, flames and huge columns of smoke rose from the site on its outskirts.
"The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. "This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed."
Russia's Defence Ministry said Ukraine had also fired Flamingo cruise missiles and said it had downed nearly 2,000 Ukrainian drones targeting various regions and 8 cruise missiles in the last 24 hours. It said it would intensify its own strikes on Ukrainian military targets in response.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Voting systems hit by cyberattacks, say officials
Voting systems also faced waves of cyber attacks, according to election authorities, who said that the electoral process had nonetheless been mostly smooth.
Russia's opposition in exile had called on those who opposed the authorities to stand in line at voting stations at noon to express their dissent, a call which saw long lines form in some locations. It was unclear, however, what impact that had on the overall outcome.
The Kremlin is likely to present the results as evidence of public backing for Putin's policies and for the war, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Read morePutin urges Russians to vote in parliamentary election as show of support for Ukraine war
Central Election Commission Chairwoman (CEC) Ella Pamfilova said the latest attacks had not deterred voters. "The more pressure they put on us, the more we are seeing an unprecedented level of what I would call public unity," RIA news agency quoted her as saying.
Turnout had reached nearly 57% as of early evening Moscow time, CEC data showed.
Most anti-war candidates have been barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko's leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party's name and the slogan "For peace".
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict - Europe's deadliest since World War Two - as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West. Moscow says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
'Pseudo election'
Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a "pseudo election".
Despite what experts see as the election's predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated "a foreign agent", said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia.
"The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot," it said in a note.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the East Sea
articles.body:
North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the East Sea
Kyiv • UNN
Pyongyang launched a short-range ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea. South Korea convened an emergency meeting.
North Korea launched one short-range ballistic missile toward the East Sea on Sunday, South Korea's military reported, several days after Pyongyang vowed to take "appropriate measures" in response to the continuation of U.S.-led military exercises in the region. Yonhap reports, writes UNN.
Details
South Korea's military said the launch was detected at approximately 3:00 p.m. local time on Sunday from the Wonsan area. The missile traveled about 450 km. An analysis is currently underway to determine the projectile's exact characteristics and other details.
The JCS said that South Korean and U.S. intelligence services had tracked the launch and exchanged relevant data from the very beginning, and had also shared information about the missile launch with Japan.
"We are closely monitoring North Korea's various activities and maintaining the capability and readiness to deliver a decisive response to any provocations within the framework of a strong joint South Korea-U.S. defense posture," the committee said.
South Korea's National Security Office (NSO) convened an emergency security meeting involving the Ministry of National Defense and the JCS to discuss the latest missile launch.
"We assessed our response posture, analyzed and evaluated the impact of the latest missile launch on our national security, and discussed appropriate measures," the office said in a statement.
The NSO called on Pyongyang to immediately cease such military activities, reminding it that ballistic missile launches violate UN Security Council resolutions banning the development of nuclear weapons and missiles.

articles.title: Russia threatens to further intensify attacks on Kyiv following hits in Moscow
articles.body:
Russia threatens to further intensify attacks on Kyiv following hits in Moscow
The Russian Ministry of Defence is threatening to intensify attacks on Kyiv following Ukrainian attacks on Moscow.
Source: Russian news agency TASS, citing Russian Ministry of Defence
Details: Reportedly "in response to attacks by Armed Forces of Ukraine on civilian infrastructure", the Russians are threatening to step up attacks "on military targets in Kyiv".
They also claim that the attempted Ukrainian attack on Moscow failed.
The Russian Ministry of Defence alleged that 1,951 Ukrainian UAVs and 8 cruise missiles were shot down over the course of the day.
For reference: Russia is in its fifth year of conducting an unprovoked full-scale war against Ukraine. Starting in 2022, attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and other targets, particularly in Kyiv, intensify every autumn. In recent weeks, Kyiv has been subjected to Russian attacks virtually around the clock, including with jet-powered UAVs and ballistic missiles.
Background:
- On the night of 19-20 September, Ukrainian drones reportedly conducted a large-scale drone attack over Moscow and Moscow Oblast. A major fire apparently broke out at the Sofyino logistics technopark and the oil refinery in Kapotnya. Additionally, the Moscow oil refinery in the Kapotnya district caught fire after a drone attack.
- On 20 September, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that the Russian capital had come under its largest drone attack to date.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the defence forces used a range of Ukrainian long-range weapons, including Flamingo, Palianytsia and Pelican, during the overnight attack on the Moscow region.
- Ukraine's General Staff has reported that three units at the Moscow oil refinery were damaged in an overnight strike. The defence forces also hit a Russian Buk-M3 air defence system, a Nebo-U radar station and a drone production site on occupied territories.

articles.title: Russia Fired 2,000 Drones and 19 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched more than 2,000 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 19 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday, Sept. 20.
Writing on Facebook, Zelensky noted that the majority of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) deployed by Russia in the weekly barrage were turbojet-powered variants, which travel at higher speeds and present increased challenges for ground-based air defenses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The president reported that Russian strikes systematically targeted civilian and critical infrastructure across the Kharkiv, Sumy, and Odesa regions over recent days, while residential buildings sustained hits in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia. He added that aerial bombardments overnight and into Sunday morning also affected the Vinnytsia, Kyiv, Zhytomyr, and Cherkasy regions.
“Ukraine is constantly looking for and finding ways to defend itself and respond to these strikes against life,” Zelensky stated.
“It is important that our partners also seek and find ways to make Russia feel its war. Right now is the right moment to take new sanctions steps against the aggressor and press for peace through strength. The US, Europe, and all G7 nations have the corresponding capabilities. We count on new, strong steps.”
Monastery drone attack and rail hits in Vinnytsia
Zelensky highlighted a targeted tactical drone strike in the Kherson region on Saturday afternoon, Sept. 19, where a Russian first-person view (FPV) drone struck an active male monastery in the village of Chervonyi Mayak within the Novoraisk community.
Russia Claims Cyberattacks Targeted Parliamentary Election Online Voting System
According to Kherson Regional Military Administration Head Oleksandr Prokudin, the drone impact killed a 71-year-old priest and injured four other clergymen aged 31, 51, 51, and 53, all of whom sustained blast and shrapnel trauma while on the monastery grounds.
In the Vinnytsia region, Russian attack drones struck a railway infrastructure facility on Sunday, Sept. 20, the State Emergency Service (SES) reported. Firefighting teams contained and extinguished the blaze, with regional authorities confirming no casualties.
The Ukrainian Air Force announced that Russian forces launched 138 unmanned aerial vehicles overnight from four launch vectors, deploying Shahed-type loitering munitions, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys.
Air defense units shot down or electronically suppressed 101 drones nationwide, while munitions impacts were recorded across 17 locations and falling debris was confirmed at five sites.
Deadly residential strikes in Kyiv region and Dnipro
The weekly tally and Sunday overnight raids follow Russian strikes targeting civilian residential infrastructure across central Ukraine late Saturday evening, Sept. 19.
In the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region, a Russian strike hit a private residence, killing a mother and her young children. According to preliminary findings by the Kyiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office, the woman had brought her children inside to put them to bed when the explosion occurred, collapsing the home’s ceilings and sparking a fire.
Concurrently on Saturday evening, Russian fire struck the Novyi Kontynent shopping center in the city of Dnipro, triggering a major commercial fire and injuring at least four civilians.
Emergency responders worked through the night to clear burning debris and inspect adjacent residential structures for structural damage.
